title: Two flashes eight years apart reveal a faraway companion
freshness: Unreviewed arXiv preprint first submitted October 9, 2026 and submitted to ApJL; preliminary and within the preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: Astronomers matched two brief gravitational microlensing events separated by 8.36 years and found that they are best explained by a single source star being lensed by a very wide binary system. The favored model points to a low-mass M dwarf with a brown-dwarf or super-Jupiter companion roughly 450 astronomical units away in projection.
whyItMatters: Very wide, low-mass companions are hard to find because they are faint and can sit far from their host stars. This system shows that long-baseline microlensing surveys can uncover companions in an orbital regime that is difficult for both transits and conventional imaging.

exploreFurther.label: Read the Yang et al. preprint

whatToExploreNext: How can repeated microlensing events distinguish a bound wide companion from two unrelated lensing events?
body:
## Two brief flashes, one possible system

Gravitational microlensing happens when the gravity of a foreground object bends and magnifies the light of a more distant star. The alignment is temporary, so most events appear as a single brightening that lasts days or weeks. OGLE-2016-BLG-0523 is unusual because its light curve shows two short-lived bumps separated by 8.36 years.

A new preprint examines whether those two brightenings came from the same physical system. The authors cross-matched microlensing events detected by the OGLE-IV and KMTNet surveys between 2011 and 2024, then tested several explanations for the pair of signals. Their favored model is a binary lens acting on one background source star.

In that interpretation, the two lensing components have very different masses and are widely separated. The measured Einstein timescales of the two bumps are 8.343 plus or minus 0.076 days and 3.231 plus or minus 0.047 days. From those timescales, the model gives a binary mass ratio of about 0.15.

## Why the companion is interesting

The team used a Bayesian analysis to estimate the physical properties of the lens system. The most likely primary is a low-mass M dwarf. The companion is probably either a low-mass brown dwarf or a super-Jupiter, categories that sit near the boundary between planets and failed stars.

The inferred projected separation is about 450 astronomical units. For comparison, Pluto orbits the Sun at roughly 39 astronomical units on average. A companion this far from a small host star would occupy an extreme part of parameter space that is difficult to probe with many other detection methods. The authors describe it as the widest low-mass object discovered through microlensing to date.

That does not mean astronomers have directly imaged the companion or measured a full orbit. The mass and separation come from lens modeling and statistical inference. Microlensing is powerful because it can reveal dark or faint objects from their gravitational effect alone, but turning a light curve into a unique physical system can involve degeneracies.

## Ruling out simpler explanations

The researchers tested three scenarios. Besides the favored binary-lens, single-source model, they considered one lens magnifying two different source stars and the possibility that the two bumps were completely unrelated microlensing events.

The binary-source explanation fit the data substantially worse. The unrelated-event explanation was disfavored by the low probability of two independent events occurring so close together, as well as problems with the combined source brightness and color implied by that model. Those tests do not eliminate every uncertainty, but they make the wide binary interpretation the strongest of the cases examined.

## A new use for long microlensing baselines

The broader lesson is methodological. Very wide companions may reveal themselves not through one complicated microlensing event, but through separate lensing signals years apart. That means old survey archives can become more valuable as their time baselines grow.

Future missions such as the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, along with proposed high-cadence microlensing surveys, should detect many more short events. Linking events separated by years could open a new route to measuring how common very wide planets and brown dwarfs are around low-mass stars.

**Measured:** two short microlensing bumps separated by 8.36 years, with event timescales of about 8.34 and 3.23 days.

**Inferred:** a low-mass M dwarf with a brown-dwarf or super-Jupiter companion at a projected separation of roughly 450 astronomical units is the favored physical interpretation.
